definitions.definition: Excitable cell that fires electrical signals and forms networks, mainly within the central nervous system.
Branched extension of a nerve cell that receives most of the cell's incoming signals, often through small spines.
Compact cell body of a nerve cell that houses the nucleus and carries out most protein synthesis.
Thin cable-like projection of a nerve cell that carries signals away from the cell body, sometimes over long distances.
Specialized junction where one cell passes a signal to another, usually through chemical messengers across a small gap.
All-or-nothing electrochemical pulse produced when a nerve cell's voltage changes enough, which then travels along its axon.
Computing model built from many connected numerical units, loosely inspired by the brain, that learns by adjusting connection strengths.
Adjustable value on a connection that sets how strongly one signal influences the next unit; changed during training.
Element that forms a weighted sum of its inputs plus an offset and adjusts its coefficients by an error-driven rule.
Numerical processing unit that sums its weighted inputs, adds an offset, and passes the result through a nonlinear function to give one output.
Term added to a unit's weighted input sum before the nonlinear output function is applied.
Nonlinear function that converts a unit's total input into its output signal.
Output rule giving 1 when the weighted input sum reaches a set level and 0 otherwise, splitting inputs with a hyperplane.
Binary unit working in discrete time steps that fires only when enough excitatory inputs are active and no inhibitory input is.
Linear binary classifier that multiplies inputs by weights, adds a bias, and applies a step function to output 0 or 1.
Property of a dataset whose classes can be divided by a single straight boundary; AND, OR and NOR have it, XOR does not.
Early single-layer network of Widrow and Hoff that computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias.
Multilayer feedforward network built from ADALINE units with a sign output, trained by special rules because the sign function cannot be differentiated.
Grossberg learning scheme, introduced in 1976, for training adaptive filters; Kohonen later used the same equation in self-organizing maps.
Grossberg learning scheme, introduced from 1967 onward, used for learning spatial patterns.
Recurrent network of two fully connected layers that, given a pattern at either layer, returns the paired pattern at the other.
Memory that links a stored vector to itself so that a partial or noisy cue settles to the full stored pattern.
Pattern of connections among neurons, forming a directed weighted graph usually organised into input, hidden and output layers.
Network in which each layer's outputs feed only the next layer, so information moves in one direction.
Forward-only network of two or more layers, able to solve problems that a single layer cannot, trained by backpropagation.
Network whose connections loop back to the same or earlier layers, so each step's output feeds into the next step.
Process of adjusting connection strengths to reduce the gap between predicted outputs and known outputs in sample data.
Principle that a connection strengthens when one cell repeatedly and persistently helps drive another cell to fire.
definitions.unitTitle: Learning Methods and Basic Learning Laws

definitions.definition: Weight-setting rule that raises a connection when the two linked units are active together and lowers it when they are not.
definitions.unitTitle: Learning Methods and Basic Learning Laws

definitions.definition: Extension in which a weight rises when it helps fire a unit, and falls when it inhibits firing or units do not fire together.
definitions.unitTitle: Learning Methods and Basic Learning Laws

definitions.definition: Iterative procedure that, on a wrong output, shifts each weight in proportion to learning rate, error and the matching input.
definitions.unitTitle: Learning Methods and Basic Learning Laws

definitions.definition: Gradient-descent learning method that adjusts the input weights of a single-layer network to reduce output error.
definitions.unitTitle: Learning Methods and Basic Learning Laws

definitions.definition: Rule used by ADALINE that moves each weight in proportion to target-minus-output error times input, minimising squared error.
definitions.unitTitle: Learning Methods and Basic Learning Laws

definitions.definition: Small constant that scales the size of each weight change in a gradient-based update.
definitions.unitTitle: Learning Methods and Basic Learning Laws

definitions.definition: Method that computes the loss gradient for each weight by passing error backward from output toward input.
definitions.unitTitle: Learning Methods and Basic Learning Laws

definitions.definition: Weight update proportional to the product of input correlations and current weights, which makes weights grow unstably.
definitions.unitTitle: Learning Methods and Basic Learning Laws

definitions.definition: Memory that, given one pattern, returns a different associated pattern which may have a different size.
Task of linking a vector with itself so that a degraded version of a stored pattern is completed.
Setting connection strengths so that a pattern becomes a stable low-energy state the network can later recall.
Memory that recovers a complete stored pattern from a partial or corrupted cue.
Grouping observations into categories using an algorithm built from their measurable properties.
Unsupervised scheme in which nodes compete to respond to inputs, each specializing so similar patterns are grouped.
Selection mechanism in which only the strongest-responding unit becomes active while the others stay off.
Unsupervised network trained by competition that turns high-dimensional data into a low-dimensional, usually two-dimensional, map preserving structure.
Map node whose weight vector lies closest to a given input; it and its neighbours are pulled toward that input.
Function whose value depends only on the distance from a centre point, commonly Gaussian in shape.
Three-layer network with an input layer, a nonlinear hidden layer of distance-based units, and a linear output layer.
Distance-based unit whose response falls off exponentially with squared distance from its centre, scaled by a decay parameter.
Vector at which a hidden unit responds most strongly, often chosen by sampling training inputs or by clustering.
Three-layer network combining Grossberg's instar and outstar learning to map m-dimensional inputs onto n-dimensional outputs.
Multilayer hierarchical network proposed by Fukushima in 1979 for pattern recognition such as handwritten characters; precursor of convolutional networks.
Neocognitron unit type that detects local features in its input.
Neocognitron unit type that tolerates small shifts in position of the features detected by the preceding layer.
Single-layer recurrent network with symmetric connections between all neurons that settles into low-energy states encoding stored patterns.
